title: API 510 Training in New Orleans: Pressure Vessel Exam Prep
description: API 510 exam prep for vessel inspectors at the Garyville, Norco, Meraux and Chalmette refineries and River Parishes plants. Self-paced, with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector Exam Prep for Greater New Orleans and the River Parishes
html:
API 510 exam prep for vessel inspectors on the river below Baton Rouge

Below Baton Rouge the Mississippi bends past Garyville, Norco, New Orleans, Meraux and Chalmette before it runs out through Plaquemines Parish to the Gulf, and almost every mile of that bank holds pressure vessels: hydrocracker reactors, coke drums, crude and vacuum towers, reformer separators, chemical columns, renewable diesel reactors and the cold drums of an LNG export plant. This page is for the people who inspect that equipment, or want the certification to sign for it, in owner-user inspection departments, inspection contractors and NDT companies.

There is no Atlantis classroom in New Orleans. The API 510 course is self-paced and online, and an instructor answers your questions while you study, so a candidate living in Metairie, LaPlace, Destrehan or Chalmette fits it around a roster rather than a timetable. The American Petroleum Institute decides who is eligible, administers the API 510 examination in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification. The course prepares you for that day; it confers nothing on its own, and Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider.

Five refineries between Garyville and Chalmette, by EIA's count

The U.S. Energy Information Administration's refinery capacity survey, which reports operable capacity at the start of 2026, lists five refineries on this reach of the river. Together they come to roughly 1.38 million barrels per calendar day of atmospheric crude distillation, more than twice the two refineries in the Baton Rouge area. The table gives crude capacity in barrels per calendar day and the downstream units, in barrels per stream day, that hold most of each site's heavy-wall vessels.

Read every column as a family of vessels with its own inspection history. Hydrocracking means heavy-wall reactors in high-pressure hydrogen, usually chromium-molybdenum steel with a stainless weld overlay, followed by hot and cold high-pressure separators. Delayed coking means drums that are heated and quenched on every cycle. Catalytic cracking means a reactor and regenerator behind refractory, with cyclones and a main fractionator. Solvent deasphalting, listed at Garyville and Meraux, means extraction towers and solvent recovery drums.

Marathon says Garyville employs more than 950 people and ships product by pipeline, barge, truck, rail and ocean tanker. PBF Energy calls Chalmette a dual-train coking refinery with a Nelson complexity of 13.0 that runs light and heavy crude and makes specialty chemicals as well as fuels. Shell dates its Norco site to 1929. Valero calls its Norco plant the St. Charles refinery, and beside it Diamond Green Diesel, a joint venture of a Valero subsidiary and Darling Ingredients, makes renewable diesel. Meraux, the smallest of the five on EIA's figures, has a hydrocracker and a deasphalting unit but no coker or catalytic cracker in the listing.

Vessels outside the refinery fence: chemicals, renewable fuel and LNG

Dow's St. Charles Operations at Hahnville, which Dow describes as a 2,000-acre integrated petrochemical complex just upriver from New Orleans, began in 1966; its fact sheet counts about 2,500 Dow and contract employees and more than 10 billion pounds a year of production capacity.

Renewable diesel adds a newer branch of the family. The 2019 announcement of Diamond Green Diesel's Norco expansion described an existing 18,000 barrel-per-day renewable diesel refinery and an expansion adding 400 million gallons a year of capacity. Its reactors and separators work in hydrogen, as hydrotreaters do, but the feeds bring a contaminant picture that a crude-based design basis never assumed, so a change of feed deserves the same fresh damage mechanism review as any other change of service.

In Plaquemines Parish, Venture Global's Plaquemines LNG began exporting cargoes in late 2024 and moved its first phase into commercial operation in 2026, with a nameplate capacity of 20 million tonnes a year. Low-temperature service puts minimum design metal temperature and brittle fracture on the inspector's list, and both are API 510 topics.

Damage mechanisms that lower-river vessels teach

The Body of Knowledge for your exam window lists the API RP 571 mechanisms that can be examined, so start there. Most of them can be pinned to a unit somewhere between Garyville and the river mouth, which is a practical way to remember them:

  • High temperature hydrogen attack and temper embrittlement. Hydrocracker and hydrotreater reactors in chromium-molybdenum steel. RP 571 describes both, and points to API RP 941 for the operating limits that govern hydrogen attack.
  • Wet H2S damage. Blistering, hydrogen-induced cracking and stress-oriented cracking in coker and FCC gas plants, sour water strippers and amine units, found with wet fluorescent magnetic particle testing and angle-beam ultrasonics rather than thickness readings.
  • Thermal fatigue. Coke drums cycling between hot fill and water quench, where bulging and cracking at the skirt and shell welds develop over many cycles.
  • Erosion and refractory damage. FCC reactors, regenerators and cyclones.
  • Brittle fracture. Light-ends drums that can auto-refrigerate when depressurised, cold LNG service, and thick vessels pressure tested in cool weather.
  • Corrosion under insulation. New Orleans averages 63.4 inches of precipitation a year on NOAA's 1991 to 2020 normals, with about 115 days of wet weather, so insulated vessels stay damp, and austenitic stainless steel under wet insulation adds chloride stress corrosion cracking.

The exam never names a refinery; it describes a mechanism and asks how to find and judge it. The API 571 explainer and the guide to choosing NDE by damage mechanism go further.

Two closed-book rules, worked with river refinery numbers

Metal temperature during a pressure test. API 510 asks for the metal to be held at least 30°F above the minimum design metal temperature (MDMT) when the vessel is more than 2 in. thick, and at least 10°F above it when the vessel is 2 in. thick or less. The test temperature need not exceed 120°F unless data on the material's brittle behaviour call for a higher one.

  • A hydrotreater reactor with a 5.5 in. shell and an MDMT of 45°F: the metal must be at 75°F or warmer before pressure goes on.
  • A propane accumulator 1.25 in. thick with an MDMT of −20°F: the margin is 10°F, so −10°F is the floor, and the common mistake is applying the 30°F margin to a vessel that is not thick enough to need it.
  • A thick reactor whose MDMT is 100°F: adding 30°F gives 130°F, but the 120°F ceiling applies unless the material data argue otherwise.

Interval limits. The interval between internal or on-stream inspections may not exceed half the remaining life or 10 years, whichever is less. Where the remaining life is under four years, the interval may be the full remaining life, up to two years. An above-ground vessel gets an external visual inspection at the lesser of five years or the internal interval.

  • A cold high-pressure separator reads 1.420 in. against a required thickness of 1.285 in. and corrodes at 0.010 in. a year: remaining life is 0.135 ÷ 0.010 = 13.5 years, so the internal interval can be up to 6.75 years and the external stays at five.
  • A vacuum tower with 24 years of remaining life: half is 12 years, so the 10-year cap governs.
  • A sour water stripper feed drum with 3.2 years left: under four years, the interval may be the full remaining life, but no more than two years, and the external inspection falls due at two years as well.

Owners who set intervals by risk-based inspection under API 510 follow the assessment instead, which is the subject of API 580 study. To check your own numbers, try the inspection interval calculator, and see pressure testing after a repair for the test rules in context.

Owner-user inspection departments and the contractors around them

API 510 is written around the owner-user's inspection organisation: the group that keeps the vessel records, plans the inspections and employs or engages the authorized pressure vessel inspector who signs for them. The large refineries and chemical sites on this river keep their own inspection groups, and they bring in contract inspectors, NDT companies and engineering firms when units come down. The owner-user inspection organisation guide explains how the roles divide, and the API 510 code guide walks through the code.

API counts experience gained within the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, which includes an owner-user inspection organisation, and it verifies what you write down. Atlantis's own UT, MT, PT and VT field work on vessels around the city is described on the pressure vessel inspection page for New Orleans.

Routes into API 510 for New Orleans candidates

  • Engineers. The University of New Orleans lists ABET-accredited bachelor's programmes in civil, electrical and mechanical engineering and in naval architecture and marine engineering. A bachelor's degree or higher in engineering or technology brings the requirement down to one year of supervising or performing inspection activities as API 510 describes them.
  • Process technology graduates. Nunez Community College in Chalmette and River Parishes Community College, with campuses that include Reserve and St. Charles, both offer a 60-credit associate of applied science in process technology. API asks two years of experience from holders of a two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology, one of them in inspection; whether a particular process technology degree qualifies is API's decision, so submit the transcript and let API rule.
  • NDT technicians. With a high school diploma, the requirement is three years in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of pressure vessels, including one year supervising or performing inspection. Atlantis's ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT training in New Orleans covers the methods that build that record.
  • Welders and fitters. Repair and construction work counts towards the total, and many take AWS CWI exam prep in New Orleans before or after API 510.
  • Veterans. Three or more years of technical military service count like a bachelor's degree and two years like a two-year degree, unless the discharge was dishonorable.

Without formal education, API asks for five or more years. The full rules are on the API 510 certification requirements page.

Fitting API 510 study around river turnarounds

Turnaround season on the lower river pulls inspectors into long shifts for weeks at a time, then hands them quieter months. A self-paced course fits that rhythm. Plan the bulk of the calculation work and Section VIII reading for the quiet months, then drop to short review sessions while a unit is down, and save the timed practice papers for the final stretch before your exam window.

A useful order: choose your window from the API exam schedule and download its effectivity sheet; learn API 510's rules on intervals, repairs and rerating for the closed-book half; drill Section VIII arithmetic; finish with open-book practice in the code PDFs.

The day itself runs to 7.5 hours. You face 170 questions, of which 140 are scored and 30 are unscored pretest items, split into 110 closed-book and 60 open-book questions, with a short tutorial, 2.75 hours for the closed-book part, a 45-minute lunch and 3.75 hours for the open-book part, where the code PDFs are on the computer and nothing else is allowed in. Prometric lists test centres in and around New Orleans, and you book one after API accepts your application.

How New Orleans candidates usually prepare, and where each route falls short

  • Learning inside a plant inspection group. Unbeatable for judgement and real vessel files, but rarely covers every document in the Body of Knowledge or open-book technique.
  • A classroom seminar in another city. A concentrated block, at the cost of travel, release from the roster and a pace set for the room.
  • Studying the code books alone. Cheap and flexible, but nobody settles a clause that reads two ways, and calculations tend to be under-practised.
  • The Atlantis self-paced online course. Structured lessons, worked calculations, practice papers and an instructor to answer questions, around your shifts; you still have to set your own deadlines.

Sponsoring API 510 candidates from a River Parishes site

Refineries, chemical plants and contractors between LaPlace and Chalmette can enrol several candidates under one quote; fees are quoted on request. Each person still applies to API individually, with their own experience record and employer verification, and books a test centre seat when their roster allows. Groups do best when the employer checks each record against API's rules before enrolment and pairs each person with a certified inspector who knows how the site applies the code.

faq.q: Can I study for API 510 in New Orleans without travelling to a class?
faq.a: Yes. There is no Atlantis classroom in New Orleans, and the course does not need one: it is self-paced online study with an instructor who answers your questions. The only place you have to be in person is the Prometric test centre on exam day, which you book after API approves your application.

faq.q: Does inspection work on hydrocracker reactors at a Norco or Garyville refinery count toward API 510 experience?
faq.a: Reactors and separators are pressure vessels, so supervising or performing their inspection can count, provided the work falls within the last 10 years and was done for an owner-user inspection organisation or an authorized inspection agency. Describe the equipment and your actual role plainly on the application, because API verifies it with your employer.

faq.q: Will LNG plant topics from Plaquemines appear on the API 510 exam?
faq.a: Not by name. The exam tests the code and its referenced documents, not particular plants. What a cold-service inspector meets daily does appear, though: minimum design metal temperature, brittle fracture and the metal temperature rules for pressure tests are all part of what API 510 and its Body of Knowledge cover.

faq.q: I have a naval architecture degree from UNO. Which API 510 route applies to me?
faq.a: A bachelor's degree or higher in engineering or technology puts you on the shortest route: one year of supervising or performing inspection activities as described in API 510. The University of New Orleans lists its naval architecture and marine engineering bachelor's programme among its ABET-accredited degrees. The year has to be genuine inspection work within the last 10 years, and API makes the final decision.

faq.q: Does a process technology associate degree from Nunez or River Parishes shorten the experience requirement?
faq.a: API reduces the requirement to two years, one of them in inspection, for holders of a two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology. Whether a given process technology degree is accepted under that heading is API's call, so include the transcript with your application. Without it, the high school route asks for three years.

faq.q: How does a renewable diesel unit change what a vessel inspector studies?
faq.a: The code is the same: thickness, intervals, repairs and testing follow API 510 whatever the feed. What changes is the damage mechanism review, because renewable feeds carry different contaminants from crude. The exam rewards the habit of treating a change of feed as a change of service and asking which RP 571 mechanisms now apply.

faq.q: Where do New Orleans candidates take the API 510 exam?
faq.a: At a Prometric test centre; Prometric lists centres in and around New Orleans, and you choose one once API accepts your application for a window. The examination is computer-based and in person only. No books, papers or notes go into the room, and the code PDFs for the open-book part are provided on screen.

faq.q: Can a contractor working at Chalmette or Meraux enrol several inspectors together?
faq.a: Yes. An employer can sponsor a group under one quote, with fees quoted on request, and each candidate studies at their own pace with access to the instructor. Every person still makes their own application to API, with their own experience record, and API alone decides eligibility, runs the examination and issues certificates.
